Circles With Equal Chords

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Move two circles and a line, and watch a green line find equal chords in both circles. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the blue points to move the line and the circles, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names and the construction.

Drag L, O, O' or a radius point; focus one and press the arrow keys for smaller moves (Shift for bigger ones).

Look for the math

Two different circles can be crossed by one straight line so that both chords are the same length. Drag the points and the green line follows; the two chords stay equal every time a solution exists.

Slide one circle along L

Imagine cutting the first chord out and sliding that whole circle along L until the chord lands on the second circle. The centre O moves to T, where the line through O parallel to L meets the line through O' perpendicular to L. A translation keeps every length the same, so the circle centred at T with the first radius has a chord CD just like AB. Tick Show hint to see T, that dashed circle and the two construction lines. Its common chord with the second circle is CD; moving CD back gives AB.

Where the green line sits

Write the distances of O and O' from L as h₁ and h₂, and their radii as r₁ and r₂. A line at signed distance t from L cuts a chord of length 2√(r² − (h − t)²) — that is the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle from the centre to the chord. Setting the two lengths equal and cancelling the t² terms leaves the single value

t = (h₁ + h₂)/2 + (r₁² − r₂²)/(2(h₂ − h₁))

when h₁ ≠ h₂. The logic test compared this formula with the applet's construction on more than a thousand layouts, including tilted lines; the largest difference was below one millionth of a drawing unit.

One, none, or infinitely many

The page says there may be one solution, none, or — when the circles are equal and L is parallel to the line of centres — infinitely many. All three are true: on a grid of 225 distance-and-radius choices there were 38 one-solution cases, 182 with none, and 5 with infinitely many. When h₁ = h₂ the formula above has no denominator: equal radii make every parallel line work, unequal radii make none work.

One honest difference: the applet's circle-crossing helper treats nearly coincident centres as a single point, so it reports no crossing in the infinitely-many case. Our picture follows the applet's construction and shows no green line there, while the statement above follows the page and the mathematics. The applet also leaves the picture blank when a radius is under two units, when O' is within one unit of L, or when the common chord is shorter than one unit; those guards are copied here.

Tick the hint, then drag R' towards O'. Watch the dashed circle stop crossing the second one: that is exactly when the green line and both equal chords disappear.
